sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title (Philippson 2005, Pitch accent in Comorian and Proto-Sabaki tones, RMCA 2005 pp.199-220): relevant, but no open copy exists (HAL, OpenAlex, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, RMCA open-access lists, Google Books, DDL CV all checked); print only, priority high. In its place this search of works with stress in the title downloaded two first-hand open sources: Philippson's 1991 thesis (author-posted PDF at DDL Lyon; Mwali loci p.275 n.1, p.350, p.421, p.422: Comorian is 'purement accentuelle' with lexically marked syllables, and Mwali is 'à peu près identique au ngazija', having gone further in levelling verb-radical accent contrasts) and Rey 1994 'Première approche du mwali' (Persée page scan, p.170 §1.5: penultimate vowel lengthened in most words in isolation, some words carry a melodic mark on the final syllable). Both refine and confirm the catalog's tonal-or-pitch accent coding with no fixed stress rule; nothing supports a fixed-stress reclassify. Philippson 1991 p.422/p.350 is proposed as the new deciding source over Lafon 1991 + Heepe 1920.

new_statements.translation: [p.422] Mwali, another Comorian dialect, is almost identical to Ngazidja (but I have no data allowing me to assert that the themes with two marked syllables that we met in the latter dialect also exist in Mwali) [p.350] Comorian is a purely accentual language. At the lexical level, syllables divide into marked and unmarked. There is normally no more than one marked syllable per morpheme [p.275 n.1] A stage reached in the Mwali dialect, which realises: tsifungú, tsilatsá.

new_statements.reading: Mwali has the Comorian lexical pitch accent system (privative marked vs unmarked syllables, one H per prosodic group placed by post-lexical foot construction, default foot on the penult of an unmarked word in isolation), essentially the Ngazidja system; there is no fixed word-stress rule. This confirms the catalog's tonal-or-pitch accent coding and refines it toward 'pitch accent / privative accent' rather than a multi-tone system. Rey 1994 p.170 (Mwali-specific, first-hand) adds penultimate vowel lengthening in isolation and a pitch mark on the final syllable of some words. Philippson 2005 (the works with stress in the title) was not obtainable and remains the highest-priority acquisition.

The classification tonal-OR-pitch accent with no stress rule is consistent with everything reachable: Heepe marks lexical pitch on his Mwali text; Rombi 1983 p.63 (primary, downloaded now from HAL and read from the page scan) states verbatim that Comorian combines surviving tonal oppositions with accentual-intonational groups, 'avec un système tonal assez bien conservé en šimwali'; Patin 2018 treats the sister variety Shingazidja as a privative H/zero tone system drifting toward accent. Nothing found suggests a fixed-stress reclassify. sources.note: First-hand comparative analysis by the Comorian-accent specialist. p.350 §3.8: Comorian (Ndzuani data) is 'une langue purement accentuelle' with lexically marked vs unmarked syllables, at most one marked syllable per morpheme, feet built post-lexically over the prosodic group with a H on each foot's last syllable, all H but the first deleted; p.354: a word with no marked syllable gets a default foot on its penult in isolation. p.275 n.1: Mwali has gone one step further than Ndzuani in losing the underlying accentual contrast of verb radicals, realising tsifungú, tsilatsá (both final-accented)…

sources.citation: Rey, Véronique. 1994. Première approche du mwali. Africana Linguistica 11 (Annales du Musée Royal de l'Afrique Centrale, Sciences Humaines 142): 169-176. DOI 10.3406/aflin.1994.952
sources.quote: 1.5. Accent — La voyelle de la syllabe pénultième de la plupart des mots prononcés en isolation est allongée. Certains mots ont une marque mélodique sur la dernière syllabe. Dans une perspective diachronique, il sera intéressant d'établir les aboutissements des tons du proto-bantu en mwali. [The vowel of the penultimate syllable of most words pronounced in isolation is lengthened. Certain words have a melodic mark on the last syllable. From a diachronic perspective it will be interesting to establish the outcomes of the Proto-Bantu tones in Mwali.]
sources.locator: p.170, §1.5 Accent (page scan rey1994_pages/, read by eye; scanned)
sources.note: Only Mwali-specific first-hand sketch found (informant from Fomboni, 1993). §1.5 'Accent', p.170: the vowel of the penultimate syllable of most words pronounced in isolation is lengthened; certain words carry a melodic (pitch) mark on the last syllable; the Proto-Bantu tone reflexes in Mwali remain to be established. Reading: demarcative penultimate lengthening plus a lexical pitch mark on some words — a pitch accent picture, no fixed stress rule stated; refines (adds the penult-lengthening fact) rather than contradicts the catalog's tonal-or-pitch accent coding.

sources.quote: Shingazidja (and its Washili variety) only: privative /H/ vs zero tone system with long-distance shift, plus default tone insertion on the stressed penult of toneless phrases; 'Shingazidja and the other Comorian languages ... bear witness to this evolution' (tone loss). Nothing specific to Shimwali.
